extracted.intended_audience: Users and implementers of the TAM interactive mathematical system (mathematicians/programmers using TAM on RAND-Tablet/IBM-360)
extracted.subtask_description: Specification and usage rules for TAM (The Assistant Mathematician): language entities, operators, statements, input/editing via RAND-Tablet, error handling, and dictionary building for handwritten character recognition. Targets users who will write, edit, and run TAM statements and build TAM dictionaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantities in TAM are either positive or negative, integral or mixed numbers. Internally, mixed numbers are carried in double-precision, floating-point form; integers are carried in one IBM/360 word (A bytes). Therefore, effective precision is that defined for the IBM/360. Quantities may be contained in variables or arrays or expressed as constants. Most storage declaration is implied by usage. Arrays are dimensioned either implicitly or explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 3, 5.7, 1.0, 2, 0, -.37, L, 3, .45. Note effective precision equals IBM/360; be aware of integer vs floating behavior when mixing types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifiers (naming rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Variables and array Identifiers are single-letter names. The legal alphabet of TAM consists of Greek and Roman uppercase and lowercase letters. An Identifier may be made unique through the use of overscoring or underscoring. Legal overscore and underscore characters are provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of legal Identifiers: a, A, a̲ (with overscore/underscore). Subscripts used with Identifiers discriminate between class members by type. The first usage classifies an identifier as function or variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operators (available and meanings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantities may be manipulated with operators: addition (+), subtraction (-), multiplication (implicit concatenation or explicit operators like · , *), division (/), exponentiation (^), root, factorial (!), absolute value (| |), ceiling ({ }), floor ({ }), product (Π), summation (Σ), unary sign, transpose (for 2-D arrays). A special operator V is used in conjunction with setting arrays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit multiplication is allowed because identifiers are single letters. Examples: ab -> a*b; c(de) -> c*(d*e). Use V to declare/dimension/preset arrays (see assignment examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational hierarchy (precedence and parentheses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parenthesization is allowed to control parsing. In absence of parentheses, hierarchy of operation (from least to most binding) is: summation, product, addition/subtraction, multiplication/division, unary plus/minus, factorial, floor/ceiling/function call/absolute value/root/exponentiation/transpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parentheses to override defaults. Understand that factorial binds more tightly than unary sign, etc., when writing expressions in two-dimensional handwritten form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator applicability and array/matrix rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Each operator is usable when meaningful. With few exceptions (e.g., transpose applies to matrices only; (-3)! is signaled as an error), operators are usable to manipulate single constants or variables. Operators are legal when applied to arrays where an acceptable matrix or vector operation is defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and constraints: matrix inversion defined only if matrix is square; certain multiplications undefined when dimensions mismatch. One-dimensional arrays are stored and treated as row vectors, except in multiplication where left one-dimensional array is row and right is treated as column producing dot product. Check interior dimensions for multiplication and divisibility rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment statement (form and use)
rubrics_metrics.description: The assignment statement is used to set identifiable variables or arrays. Form: identifier ← expression. The expression may consist of any legal manipulation of quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A ← 3 ; B ← [matrix] (also dimension B as 2,3). Special operator V used to declare, dimension, and preset arrays: V(s,t,p) where s,t are dimensions and p is optional preset value (any legal expression). Individual array elements can be set without prior explicit dimensioning until the array is used as an entity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function definition statement (form and constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Users may define arithmetic expressions as functions. Form: f n(p1,p2,...,pm) = expression where f is an identifier, n is an optional qualifier, and p_i are optional parameters (legal identifiers). Once an identifier is used as a function name it defines a class of functions and cannot later be used as a variable or array identifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function class members are distinguished by qualifier n (e.g., G1(X)=X^2 and G2(X)=X). Parameters may reuse identifiers that also serve as variables or function names elsewhere. To exponentiate a function's return, either a2(b,c) or a(b,c)2 is permissible (embedded exponentiation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Input statement (form and behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Input statement form: □ → list where list consists of legal identifiers of simple variables or arrays separated by commas. Because TAM requests values for undefined quantities as they are encountered, user-directed input is seldom necessary, but an input statement guides order of setting quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement prompts the user for values for each element in the list in turn. If the user's response contains unknown quantities, TAM will request values for those as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Output statement (form and behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Output statement form: ' list where list consists of expressions or identifiers separated by commas. The statement causes TAM to output the values or expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an identifier in the output list is undefined, TAM will first prompt the user to input a value for it and then output it. Example: B, 3+5, results in output of B and 8 (assuming B has been defined).

rubrics_metrics.name: Loop control (forms, nesting, and usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment, input, or output statements may be iterated by following the statement with loop-control information. Loop control may be specified in three forms and loops may be nested to any level, but each loop variable in the nest must be unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form 1: i*m,...,n — i is loop variable, m initial, n terminal; increment 1. Form 2: i^m1^m2^,...,n — m1 and m2 are first two values, increment defined by n2-m1; iteration completes when i exceeds/less than n. Form 3: i^^.m1^.m2^. ... .mn — explicit successive settings; loop terminates after enumerated iterations. Examples show nesting direction (right to left) and that statement iterated may, but need not, reference loop variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Built-in functions and trig conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: TAM includes built-in functions that can be activated where a function call is permissible. Examples: sin(x), cos(x), tan(x), cot(x), arctan(x), ln(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trigonometric arguments are in radians. Function names may use any combination of upper/lowercase Roman letters (e.g., ln = LN).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inputting and editing TAM statements (RAND-Tablet workflow)
rubrics_metrics.description: TAM statements are input in hand-written two-dimensional form through a RAND-Tablet display device. TAM uses a previously constructed dictionary of patterns describing the user's handwriting characteristics and defining the recognizable character set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Startup prompts for dictionary file. TAM displays pushbuttons (e.g., Exit, Erase). The line is parsed and an encoded form appears. A history display holds last four legal lines and associated output; any of these can be recalled for editing and reoperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pushbuttons and editing operations
rubrics_metrics.description: TAM provides pushbuttons to control editing and interpreter actions: Erase, Move (open-up, close-up, move-character), Context, Process (send current characters to Interpreter), Backward, Forward, Quit, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move operations described: Open-up inserts space by single horizontal line; Close-up deletes space by two horizontal lines; Move-character encloses characters in circle/rectangle and a line indicates displacement. Context handles logically attached characters (e.g., superscripts). Process sends the current user characters to the interpreter and updates history if not error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconstrained TAM: minimum declaration principle
rubrics_metrics.description: One design goal is to free the user from unnecessary or ordered declaration of storage, quantities, or functions. An array need not be explicitly dimensioned until used as an entity; identifier class (function or variable) is determined by first usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an array is used element-by-element, no explicit dimensioning needed. Before array is first used as a whole, the user must dimension it; TAM will demand values for unset elements as needed. Identifiers with overscores/underscores are classified separately based on usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand input behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: TAM requests values for quantities only when they are used (demand input). For example, A ← 2 + Y as first statement causes TAM to request value for 2? (i.e., expression elements) and then prompt for Y if unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If user response contains unknown quantities, TAM requests those in turn. Once all quantities defined, assignment completes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural expression features (implicit multiplication and embedded exponentiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: TAM allows natural mathematical notation often disallowed in programming languages: implicit multiplication and embedded exponentiation in function calls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit multiplication examples: ab → a*b; c(de) → c*(d*e); ij! → i*(j!). Embedded exponentiation: sin(a)2 → (sin(a))2 or sin2(a) → (sin(a))2. Note: implicit multiplication rules reference single-letter identifiers and superscripts/subscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: User error detection and messages
rubrics_metrics.description: TAM legality checks each statement before execution. If an illegality is discovered, the statement is rejected and an appropriate message is generated. The most frequent message: 'SYNTAX ERROR AT CHARACTER XX' (XX is character position). Other messages include TYPE ERR, CLASS ERR, X! X * INTEGER ≥ 0, OPERATION ERR - ARRAY/VECTOR, PARAMETER ERR, SUBSCRIPTS MUST BE INTEGERS, SINGULAR MATRIX, LOG OF - OR 0 ARG RETURNS -INFINITY, SYMBOL OR STRING TOO LONG, MISMATCHED DIMENSIONS, EXPONENT OVERFLOW/UNDERFLOW, SIGNIFICANCE EXCEPTION, FLOATING DIVIDE EXCEPTION, FLOAT/-. NO., etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Messages convey precise meanings: TYPE ERR for misuse of identifier as function vs variable; CLASS ERR for class misuse; OPERATION ERR when operator meaningless for arrays/vectors; PARAMETER ERR when function call parameter count mismatches; mismatched dimensions signal invalid array arithmetic. Use messages to debug user input and correct expression/usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreter errors (internal failures and response)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpreter error messages signal internal TAM Interpreter errors that should not normally appear. Examples: AN UNDEFINED ROUTINE HAS BEEN CALLED, BAD CAR, BAD CDR, GENERATOR DOES NOT MATCH ITS PARAMETERS, ALL BOOLEANS OF AN EXPRESSION ARE FALSE, BAD CADDDR, BAD COMPRESS OF ATOM, BAD OUTNUM2, COMPILER ERROR HALT, NOT ENOUGH SPACE, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such a message is encountered, the program will stop; take a register and core dump and contact TAM maintenance personnel. These indicate internal faults rather than user input issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity-overload errors and remediation
rubrics_metrics.description: Messages that capacities of TAM have been exceeded cause program stop. Examples: FULL UNDEFINED STACK, FULL BACKUP STACK, FULL ARGUMENT STACK, NO MORE ARRAY SPACE, NOT ENOUGH ARRAY SPACE, NOT ENOUGH LIST SPACE, NO MORE LARGE NUMBER SPACE, NO MORE REAL NUMBER SPACE, NO MORE GENSYM SPACE, NOT ENOUGH STRING SPACE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If encountered and excess seems unwarranted or ill defined, take a core and register dump and contact TAM maintenance personnel. These are operational capacity limits to be monitored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Building a TAM dictionary (requirements and workflow)
rubrics_metrics.description: To operate TAM, the user must have built a dictionary of recognizable characters (handwriting patterns). Each character to be used with TAM must be entered into the dictionary. A program BUILDER is provided to create or modify dictionaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Builder prompts 'CONTINUE W/ OLD DICT? Y/N'. Functions available: Save, Build, Test, Sumry, Print, Quit. Sampling mode: input strokes, dictionary matching, define/undefine display. Define strokes by circling them and touching corresponding keyboard character. Save requires file identification; include 'N' for new file; successful save prints 'DICT SAVED'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictionary keyboard sets and threshold controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Dictionary building uses keyboard pushbuttons selecting character sets: 'S' for special characters, 'G' for Greek, 'N' for numerals, 'U' for upper-case Roman alphabet, 'L' for lower-case Roman alphabet. Threshold pushbuttons 'RT' (reduced thresholds) and 'IT' (increased thresholds) control matching tolerance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduced thresholds are in effect initially; increasing thresholds may produce more matches. Use 'Redefn' to change existing definitions, 'Forget' to ignore previous action, 'Erase' to clear and sample again, 'Exit' to leave Build mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parser-generated and user input character codes (reference requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appendices provide character code mappings: Appendix B lists parser-generated characters with hex/octal/decimal and parse symbols; Appendix C lists legal user input characters and octal/hex codes. These mappings define which string/parser-generated characters and user characters are recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the code tables when building dictionaries and interpreting encoded parsed forms; parser-generated special symbols indicate structure (e.g., overscore, superscript, matrix separators, fraction line). Consult tables when debugging parsing/encoding issues.
